claims.text: The initial material is equiatomic FeNiCrMn with a single-phase FCC crystal structure.
The initial material has a controlled vacancy-cluster density.
Tensile loading is applied along both <11-1> and <110> orientations.
The applicable strain-rate range is 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
The simulations use an NVT molecular-dynamics environment at temperatures from cryogenic to room temperature.
Vacancy clusters serve as preferential nucleation sites for Shockley partial dislocations.
Shockley partial dislocations form intrinsic stacking faults on {111} planes.
At high strain rates, insufficient time for vacancy annihilation causes vacancy clusters to accumulate.
Vacancy clusters locally reduce the activation barrier for Shockley-partial nucleation.
The <11-1> orientation has a higher Schmid factor or stronger geometric constraint for partial-dislocation glide than <110>.
Partials and intrinsic stacking faults require a higher applied stress in the <11-1> orientation, while <110> facilitates easier slip.
The HCP-like regions are transient intrinsic stacking faults rather than a thermodynamic phase transformation.
High stacking-fault energy stabilizes the proposed transient intrinsic stacking faults.
The <11-1>-oriented sample will have a higher peak yield stress than the <110>-oriented sample.
Dislocation-nucleation events will be spatially correlated with vacancy clusters.
HCP-like regions will retain lattice parameters consistent with the faulted FCC matrix and will lack long-range martensitic order.
In a standard FeNiCrMn control without intentional vacancy clustering, nucleation occurs at grain boundaries or surface defects rather than at bulk vacancy clusters.
The standard <110>-oriented control has a lower yield stress than the <11-1>-oriented vacancy-clustered sample.
A distinct HCP phase can be discriminated from an FCC stacking fault by lattice-parameter measurements and diffraction showing phase-specific reflections rather than fault-related streaking.

contradictions.description: The orientation argument invokes a higher Schmid factor as a reason that <11-1> requires a higher applied stress. Without an independently established increase in critical resolved shear stress, a higher Schmid factor would ordinarily imply that a given resolved shear stress is reached at a lower applied stress, so the stated causal explanation is internally incoherent.
